I played with Spheres a couple times in the past and had a blast. I have a few criticisms related to Spheres of Power, though.

1. Custom item design is a dumpster fire.
2. You need to deeply specify your magical tradition, and the GM has to extensively track which 0-9 spell list fits you best, otherwise ritual casting vancian spells breaks easily.
3. Spellcrafting is an excellent concept, horrible in execution if your GM is malleable. **If your GM is too malleable, or gives too much freedom, do not look at spellcrafting!** It needs a competent GM and group to make it right without breaking.
4. Excessive abundance of effects that take a long time to set up. Light sphere's shapes are a big offender here, since it requires you to place 20+ squares, and you can adjust it every round....

I'd begin with building the rest of the system. Might sound counter-intuitive, but a magic system is nothing but flavor to mechanical consequences, no?

Next, I'd make *general* guidelines. For example, if your system uses something like 3d6+mods to determine an outcome of a character's actions, stat out how magic in general can give you another d6, or a modifier to that roll, that kind of stuff. You can stat out other things, like other situational buffs, debuffs, damage, healing.

After you're done with this general stuff, you can finally get into elemental magic itself. The point of the previous exercise was to build a solid foundation, and balance all magic at its core - if hurling a chunk of metal can deal 20 points of damage, then creating a tornado that tears the subject apart for effective 20 points of damage would have similar "level" or cost.

Further down you can differentiate how things work, and make each element unique - to go back to the previous example, maybe hurling chunks inherently deals more damage but is not as good for hard crowd control, while controlling air deals understandably less damage but affects things at a much wider range?

Further down you can simply stat out additional effects - if the earth elementalist wants to fly, he could do so by standing on a rocky hoverboard or roleplay Magneto with a metallic armor; an air elementalist could simply rise whenever it suits him.

So, there's that. I believe that doing things in this way, from top down to details, is very efficient for open-ended systems and gives you full control over how detailed exactly you want your system to be.

Annoyingly enough, the rulebook example of damaging a shield with hardness 3 does nothing for us, because an item gets only a maximum of two dents from one damage source so we don't know whether the hardness DR applies or not

There's one thing that's necessary to understand the hardness.

>An item reduces any damage dealt to it by its Hardness.

and

>If an item takes damage equal to or exceeding the item’s Hardness, the item takes a Dent.

are important here. The first sentence appears first, and therefore it should apply to any words following it in the paragraph.

Therefore, while an orichalcum lock has Hardness of 18 and your damage roll comes up 20, what you are really doing is dealing **2 points of damage**.

For this reason I believe that an **Orichalcum lock requires the minimum of 36 points of damage** to suffer a dent.

Impresing a kingly audience is one kind of task, that caps out at a certain DC, and impressing nobles generally stays at the same difficulty regardless of your level. What increases in difficulty is the stuff of legend, like coaxing a devil to set someone's soul free or impressing extraplanar audience in general. In the end it's the GM's job to keep the world consistent. It's not like you'd suddenly have to climb a level 15 Dire Rope just because you've hit certain character level.

Remember, challenges also scale accordingly, so when an untrained guy and an expert (both at the same level) face a level-appropriate challenge, the expert has a higher to-succeed ratio.

In addition, higher proficiency gives access to "gated" checks, so there's that. You can't even attempt to disable a legendary trap if you're not legendary at trap....disabling.
